author: smimon
text:
I'll probably avoid going short on CJ and UJ at the same time again in future.

When trading any crosspair, it's important to consider whether it's moving in one direction solely because of the strength or weakness of only one of its constituents. ITs often like to play currencies as a whole to my knowledge, rather than focusing on individual pairs. The best trades come when one part is weak and the other part is strong, resulting in swift movements.

CJ and UJ obviously share JPY as a common component. Any strength in JPY will therefore push them lower. However, CAD and USD are almost opposing currencies -over 80% of the value of the trade-weighted CADX index comes from USDCAD. Therefore usually as USD moves up, CAD moves down, and vice versa.

For this reason, we can see that the only way CJ and UJ will both go down convincingly is in the event of significant JPY strength. If JPY remains neutral, then the sole driver of the pairs will be USD, meaning that if UJ starts going down in the face of JPY neutrality, then CJ will start going up.

Which is essentially what's happening to my 2 trades up the moment, see-sawing off each other. A strong kick from JPY will push them both down, but I've effectively bet 50% against myself.

A good way to look at things is in triplets of pairings. Let's say EURUSD is going down in HTF trend - we therefore know that USD is stronger than EUR. Let's also say however that GBPUSD is headed up in HTF trend. GBP is stronger than USD. Logic then dictates that the strongest moves should be coming short on EURGBP. USD is stronger than EUR, but GBP is stronger than USD, and so therefore far stronger than EUR.

This is of course all academic, and it's possible to trade the currency pairs perfectly well in isolation, but it's always worth bearing in mind so you not only don't bet against yourself, but also so that you can pick up on something that's really looking like it's going to run.

author: smimon
text:
Well, end of the week, and I feel perhaps this is the week I've turned the corner. Demo account up about 130%, but could have been much more... Baby steps.

Things I've learned this week:

set conservative targets - going for the Hollywood trade when there are 7 obstacles between you and the target rarely pays, unless you've got your HTF analysis down to a T including the supply/demand zone that formed the level you are trying to trade off within your drawn zones eliminates any chance of being caught by the FO, at the expense of a wider stop - but better to have the win for 1 or 2R less, than getting stopped out and getting nothing

make sure we've got "room to trade into" - if you think you've seen a FL/FTR engulfed, double check what the "engulf" has gone into - is it merely another possible reaction zone? Or is it clear space in the form of CP, or a big LQ candle between you and the next PAZ? (although always watch out for SR flips we've momo'd over in the latter case)

Things to work on next week:

fear (or another manifestation of greed as I read somewhere) - after I've made one decent trade for the day and got the account nicely up, I'm freezing, spotting perfectly good trading opportunities and then not taking them, because winning is still a novelty, and I'm desperate not to go back to losing all the time again. Got to become mechanical - see the trade, take the trade. Ego preservation needs to be killed! get my HTF analysis more in order - I've missed some monster moves because I misread HTF. Essentially, I seem to be able to read LTF quite well at this point, and it's exactly the same principle - as I saw IF say way back on Pedini's journal, when looking at the W1 chart - "what would you expect to happen next if this was a M5 chart?"

Have a good weekend all.

I wanted to add some ideas for consideration on this one. I can see two options that allows one to be conservative but help maximize returns.

1. Expect the FO zone on the other side of the supply/demand and only trade that. In other words, instead of picking the entry in the supply zone, pick the entry in the FO zone above the supply. You will missing some trades but you will have a smaller stop loss to deal with.

2. The other idea is a hybrid of your style and my #1. Trade a portion of your risk at the supply zone and another portion in the FO zone. I spent a lot of time reading the FO or Engulf thread in the Homework room and it dawned on me that often price will FO to the decision point on the other side of the most recent supply/demand zone. So, why not play 2 trades. One at the edge of the obvious zone (S or D) and another in the DP beyond the S/D zone. Essentially if you had $100 to risk per trade and you see a nice supply zone with a FO area above, well, you take a $50 position near the edge of the supply zone and another $50 near the DP of the FO zone. That way you get a chance for 2 tickets to the party.

Hope that makes sense.

GJ.

Please note that I am still demo trading and not being very successful picking entries but I think I am pretty good at money management and so I hope this helped.

author: smimon
text:
Hello pal. Very interesting points. I suppose that the overall profitability of each approach depends on how often as a %age the FO happens, which isn't something I'm currently able to make even a rough guess about. From what I've seen so far - it happens more often than not.

Therefore, I think the approach you mentioned in 2 is probably the best one for taking entries on a zone combined with it's FO zone. M1 PA almost always shows the way as we get into these regions. Seeing a succession of dojis or inverted wicks is usually good enough for me to take the trade at the level I'm looking at.

author: smimon
text:
Sluggish start to the week coming up news-wise, and we quite often see a ECB/NFP "hangover" on the Monday afterwards. However that said, there are FLs and FTRs aplenty to work with on M15/M30 for nice M1 trades on any day no matter how slow, usually good for 3R or more, so even if nothing big sets up, there's always plenty profits to be had.

I like to be at my PC ready to trade the London open at 0800 GMT, since you quite often see some nice setups forming between 0600 - 0800 which get a burst of movement at 0800. My "fear of missing out" is rapidly deserting me, since even monitoring maybe 8 charts, there's always something to trade every hour if you keep your eyes peeled, and really if you're confident enough to trade at 4% risk, you only need one trade a day to compound your account into something silly in a pretty short space of time.
